paragraph_content.content: It Takes Two to Make a Revolution: Initiate at OW

We initiate coverage on TNGX with an OW rating and a Dec-2026 price target of $46. Following its monotherapy PoC last year with lead PRMT5i vopimetostat, Tango is leading the way in PDAC and potentially NSCLC through its combo trials with RAS inhibitors daraxonrasib and zoldonrasib. The first look at the combo data earlier this year with RVMD's dara showed impressive response previously unheard of in the 2L+ PDAC setting with a 92% ORR and 6-month PFS rate of 90% in a setting where, until recently, median OS was ~6 months and ORR of 10%-15%.

With combo data in hand, a Ph 3 trial in 1L PDAC is in the works, pending regulatory feedback, to gain a lead over competition, which is also collaborating with RASi players. Tango is also hedging its bets in this setting with a recently announced collaboration with ERAS. With the pipeline now streamlined to focus solely on MTAP-deleted cancers, TNG456, Tango's CNS-penetrant PRMT5i is in the clinic targeting glioblastoma, which is another difficult to treat indication, and if monotherapy PoC is shown later this year, a combo with LLY's CDK4/6i will follow. Net-net, Tango remains true to its name, with multiple disruptive combo tx options in the works targeting MTAP-deleted cancers. Initiate OW.

- PRMT5i + RASi combos have the potential to change PDAC treatment. Data for the vopi combo with RVMD's dara showing a 92% ORR in 2L+PDAC is a meaningful step above dara's 30%-35% recently seen in Ph 3 RASolute 302 which is considered a revolution in 2L PDAC. While still early, excitement is meaningful as ~22% of the ~66K annual US PDAC cases have MTAP-deletion driving Tango to plan a Ph 3 1L PDAC trial to be finalized in 2H.

- Tango isn’t putting all its eggs in one basket and is diversifying across the RASi space. The vopi combo with RVMD’s dara and zoldon is leading the way in this new combo paradigm, but neither intends to be exclusive as this new space shapes up. As RVMD is also collaborating with competitor BMY’s navlimetostat, Tango has entered a collaboration with ERAS (covered by Anupam Rama), RVMD’s lead competitor, hedging their bets in the RASi space to ensure vopi will be in the lead as it plays out.

- GBM through TNG456 has strong preclinical rationale with combo next step. Monotherapy data is expected this year from the Ph 1/2 trial in GBM (~45% delMTAP) with brain-penetrant TNG456. Initial PoC will trigger part 2 combining TNG456 with abemaciclib, LLY's CDK4/6i. This could open up another combo front for a non-overlapping MOA in a setting that is ripe for new treatment options, which we believe isn't getting value from investors just yet.

Competition in the monotherapy setting for MTAP-deleted tumors is tough, however, Tango has an opportunity to differentiate itself as the first to show such strong combination data. title_content.content: Vopimetostat is Part of a Next Generation of PRMT5 Inhibitors Following Many Years of Development and Failure

paragraph_content.content: Vopimetostat was developed as a second generation PRMT5i by Tango, following the discontinuation of TNG908 which was itself part of a new wave of MTA-cooperative

PRMT5is. Earlier PRMT5is worked through less selective mechanisms of action, such as substrate competition, which would inhibit PRMT5 but would not differentiate between healthy and tumor cells, creating a very limited therapeutic window. However, since MTAP-deleted tumors represent such a meaningful portion of all tumors (10%-15%), work continued to develop better, more selective, PRMT5 inhibitors and Tango's drugs are a result of this decades-long effort.

The ability of vopimetostat, TNG456 and other assets to bind and inhibit PRMT5 in the presence of high levels of MTA, which is a direct result of MTAP deletion, allows to differentiate between healthy and tumor cells, widely expanding the therapeutic window with a tolerable safety profile that opens up combination options, which has now become Tango's modus operandi.

title_content.content: Combos and More Combos! Brain-Penetrant TNG456 Proof-of-Concept Coming This Year and a CDK4/6i Combo Soon After

paragraph_content.content: Beyond the combination opportunity with RAS inhibitors in PDAC and NSCLC, Tango also has an ongoing Ph 1/2 trial in glioblastoma with brain-penetrant TNG456 and monotherapy data expected this year. Preclinical data has shown a lot of promise and the opportunity in this indication is meaningful with up to

of cases originating from MTAP-deleted tumors. Tango has a collaboration agreement with Eli Lilly and if monotherapy data shows any promise (in an indication with very few treatment options), Tango has said they will initiate the second portion of the study which will combine TNG456 with abemaciclib, LLY's CDK4/6i. While it remains to be seen if this combination will play out in the clinic, the fact that MTAP deletion almost exclusively occurs in the setting of CDKN2A/B deletion, rendering cells sensitive to CDK4/6 inhibition, opens up another interesting combination approach for non-overlapping MOAs in another setting that is ripe for new options.

title_content.content: Focusing on PRMT5 and Combinations: Tango is Hyper-focused with a Leaner Pipeline

paragraph_content.content: Until earlier this year, Tango still had assets in its pipeline with targets beyond PRMT5, such as HBS1L (TNG961) and CoREST (TNG260), however, it recently deprioritized these assets and streamlined the pipeline to focus solely on the PRMT5i opportunity with vopimetostat and TNG456. This follows the promising monotherapy and combination data seen for vopimetostat and the large opportunities they present. Both TNG260 and TNG961 have been deprioritized and we see this as a smart move, allowing the company to execute on the combo opportunities with its PRMT5is by expanding clinical trials to multiple combinations (RAS, CDK4/6 and potentially MAT2A), collaborations (RVMD, ERAS and LLY) and to gain potential differentiation over competition in the space.

title_content.content: Vopimetostat and TNG456 - Next Generation MTA-Cooperative PRMT5 Inhibitors

paragraph_content.content: Tango's MTA-cooperative PRMT5i program was built around the synthetic-lethality relationship, progressing from the earlier stage TNG908 to Vopimetostat (formerly TNG462) and CNS-penetrant TNG456. TNG908 was developed as a brain-penetrant MTA-cooperative PRMT5 inhibitor for MTAP-deleted cancers, including CNS tumors. Vopimetostat and TNG456 were designed as next-generation PRMT5is with enhanced potency, selectivity, and PK properties to improve target coverage and enable broader, deeper antitumor activity in MTAP-deleted solid tumors. While in preclinical work, TNG908 showed a 15x selectivity for MTAP deleted cells, vopimetostat showed 45x selectivity, and a more potent growth inhibition. For a while both vopimetostat and '908 were in clinical evaluation, however, in November 2024, following promising activity in NSCLC and PDAC, vopimetostat replaced '908 in the clinic for non-CNS tumors. At the same time, Tango unveiled TNG456, which has shown a 55x selectivity for MTAP deletion in preclinical work with high CNS penetration. In May 2025, the first patient was dosed in TNG456's Ph 1/2 trial in MTAP-deleted tumors with a focus on GBM.

title_content.content: A Short Primer on MTAP Deletion and PRMT5 As a Target in Cancer

paragraph_content.content: Methylthioadenosine phosphorylase (MTAP) is an enzyme encoded on chromosome 9p21, adjacent to the tumor suppressor gene CDKN2A and because of this genomic proximity, MTAP is almost exclusively co-deleted with CDKN2A in human cancers. MTAP loss is observed in a broad range of solid and hematologic malignancies and is generally estimated to occur in approximately 10%–15% of all human cancers. Most importantly, MTAP deletion occurs in ~22% of PDAC, ~13% of NSCLC and ~45% of GBM.

title_content.content: The Roles of MTAP and PRMT5 in the Cell

paragraph_content.content: MTAP normally participates in the methionine salvage pathway by metabolizing 5'-methylthioadenosine (MTA) back into methionine. Normal cells do not accumulate high levels of MTA, and PRMT5 can continue using the methyl-donor SAM (S-adenosylmethionine) to perform its normal function. PRMT5 catalyzes symmetric

dimethylation of arginine residues on histones and non-histone proteins and regulates processes central to tumor cell viability, including transcription, chromatin remodeling, RNA splicing, signal transduction, ribosome biology, and cell-cycle progression. When MTAP is deleted, MTA accumulates intracellularly and partially inhibits protein arginine methyltransferase 5 (PRMT5) and so the cell is more reliant on exogenous methionine.

title_content.content: The MTA-Cooperative MoA of Most Current PRMT5is

paragraph_content.content: PRMT5 is an essential protein, and so non-selective first-generation PRMT5 inhibitors (PRMT5i) had limiting therapeutic windows with associated hematopoietic toxicity. However, when MTAP is deleted, MTA accumulates, forms a complex with PRMT5 and partially inhibits it. A drug that can bind to PRMT5 only with MTA could lead to cell death, but only in cells with high MTA levels, leading to much better selectivity over healthy cells. In cells with MTAP deletion, PRMT5 is already partially inhibited due to the elevated MTA levels, opening up the possibility of synthetic lethality and sparing of wild-type cells through the development of MTA-cooperative PRMT5 inhibitors, a newer class designed to exploit MTA accumulation. Vopimetostat, and almost all current competitors are MTA-cooperative inhibitors.

title_content.content: What are the Highest Value Indications for Vopimetostat?

paragraph_content.content:
PDAC - Highest Prevalence and a Real Opportunity to Take Part in a Revolution
Despite recent advances in targeting KRAS for PDAC (see our work on RVMD), there still exists a significant need to improve outcomes for patients with one of the most deadly cancers. There are an estimated ~66K new pancreatic cancer cases annually in the US, and PDAC comprises at least 90% of pancreatic cancers, followed by neuroendocrine tumors, according to the American Cancer Society. Despite the recent Ph 3 success for daraxonrasib, doubling OS in 2L PDAC and as we await survival data from 1L trials, we need to remember that ORR in this patient population was still only ~30% leaving much room for improvement. While PDAC isn’t one of the most common cancer types, it is one of the leading causes of cancer death in the U.S. The lethality of PDAC is multifactorial but mostly based on the inability to detect the disease in early stages before it has metastasized. This late stage diagnosis leads to a 5-year survival rate of 3% within those with metastatic disease (and this is after doubling in the past decade, but before RAS inhibitors).
Despite the recent success of daraxonrasib, which is awaiting approval, treatment options for PDAC are fairly limited and not effective: only

of PDAC patients are eligible for surgery due to the advanced stage of the disease at diagnosis. Aside from late diagnosis, there are also risks related to tumor proximity to major vasculature and the lasting impact of removing the pancreas. Even in resection-amenable patients,

will develop recurrence within 2 years. Thus, clinical care for metastatic PDAC relies on systemic chemo. One of the key chemo regimens is FOLFIRINOX (FFX; a combo of 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), leucovorin, irinotecan, and oxaliplatin) with the second being a combo of gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel (GnP). For progressors, 2L regimens include irinotecan with 5-FU. Following the success of RVMD in the space, there are now dozens of new KRAS-mutant and multi/pan-RAS targeting assets in the clinic with multiple Ph 3 trials assessing their efficacy in 1L PDAC in combination with or without chemotherapy.

Initially, Tango was targeting the MTAP-deleted PDAC population and was planning on starting a Ph 3 trial in 2L MTAP-deleted PDAC, which represents 19%-32% of the PDAC population, according to sources. However, following the recent success of the combo data with multi-RAS inhibitor daraxonrasib, focus is now shifting to starting a Ph 3 pivotal trial in 1L PDAC MTAP-deleted patients in combination with daraxonrasib. In PDAC, there is no need to focus on KRAS mutational status as >90% of cases are KRAS mutated and daraxonrasib is active in WT KRAS as well. Additionally, genomic landscape work has shown a co-mutation rate of ~94% in PDAC. Thus, MTAP-deletion is the only limiting inclusion factor.

title_content.content: NSCLC: The Blueprint for Targeted Therapy

paragraph_content.content: Lung cancer is the second most common type of cancer diagnosed worldwide. The classification of lung cancer has undergone major changes over the years, as evidenced by the increased use of sequencing to classify cancer histology and a shift towards targeted therapy guided by driver mutation characterization. The two main types of lung cancer are non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and small cell lung cancer (SCLC). NSCLC is the most common form, accounting for 80% to 85% of all lung cases, and is further sub-classified into three subtypes: (1) adenocarcinoma, (2) squamous cell carcinoma and (3) large cell carcinoma, which are differentiated based on the tissue of origin.
Adenocarcinoma is the most common form, accounting for
\sim
40% of cases. In adenocarcinoma, the tumor forms in the outer region of the lung where mucus-producing cells reside. In squamous cell carcinoma, which makes up
\sim

25%-30% of cases, the cancer forms in the central part of the airway, in the lining of the bronchi. Squamous cell carcinoma is more common in older adults and smokers. Unlike the other two, large cell carcinoma is much rarer, less centralized, and can be found anywhere in the lungs.
The American Cancer Society estimates the annual incidence of lung cancer cases to be
\sim 230\mathrm{K}
. The five-year survival rate for all NSCLC is

, but it further worsens as patients enter the advanced stages. Once a tumor is spotted in the lungs, a tissue biopsy is conducted to determine the type of cancer and its stage, while next-generation sequencing is used to determine its genetic signature and the presence of oncogenic driver mutations, which is especially important for Tango's strategy as it will be targeting only tumors with MTAP deletion.

NSCLC treatment is dependent on the mutational characteristics of the tumor. There are multiple types of approved targeted therapies for NSCLC, including inhibitors targeting EGFR, ALK and ROS1 rearrangements, KRAS G12C, MET exon 14, BRAF V600E, RET fusions, HER2 and more being added annually. Absent actionable mutations, 1L treatment is based on the KEYNOTE-189 protocol including Pt-based chemotherapy with immune checkpoint blockade and is dependent on PD-L1 expression levels.
In a large molecular landscape profiling study of NSCLC, MTAP deletion was present in
\sim

13% of cases out of almost 30K samples. Not surprisingly, as they are adjacent on the 9p21 chromosome, the most common co-mutations were CDKN2A and CDKN2B with 98% and 95%, respectively, and TP53 with 63%. Next up were all types of KRAS mutations with 29%. Taken together, co-occurrence of a KRAS mutation with an MTAP-deletion occurs in
\sim
4% of NSCLC cases (Kumar et al.). While seemingly low, with
\sim
190K cases of NSCLC a year in the US, this still amounts to
\sim
25K NSCLC MTAP-deletion cases a year and
\sim
7K with a KRAS co-mutation or
\sim
17K/5K stage III/IV cases.

title_content.content: The Case for Co-Targeting PRMT5 with Other Targets

paragraph_content.content: MTAP-loss occurs almost exclusively as part of 9p21 chromosomal loss with co-deletions of CDKN2A and CDKN2B. Prior genomic studies, and even commercial panels, have not always tested specifically for MTAP-loss, making it challenging to perform retrospective studies on the clinical outcomes of patients with tumors harboring MTAP-loss. Testing for CDKN2A and CDKN2B is nearly ubiquitous, though, and this finding allows us to extrapolate the presence of MTAP-loss or perform dedicated testing for MTAP-loss in select scenarios.
Although current MTAP-loss clinical trials are investigating MAT2A or PRMT5 inhibitors as monotherapy, combination targeted therapy may ultimately prove more efficacious.

Building on the improved safety profile seen with the MTA-cooperative PRMT5is, combining them with other targeted cancer therapeutics makes sense, especially since MTAP-deleted tumors often harbor additional actionable oncogenic drivers that can be inhibited in parallel, opening up the possibility to improve on the monotherapy data seen with vopimetostat and competitors.
An especially strong rationale exists for combining KRASi with PRMT5i in MTAP deleted PDAC, where

of all tumors are KRAS mutation-driven, which is believed to be the founding oncogenic event, while CDKN2A/MTAP deletion is another frequent early alteration. PRMT5 inhibition and KRAS inhibition largely affect distinct signaling networks, but their downstream consequences converge on essential tumor processes such as MYC signaling, cell-cycle control, DNA and RNA biology, translation, interferon signaling, and apoptosis. Because these mechanisms are at least partly nonoverlapping, combinations may deepen responses, delay resistance, and produce more durable tumor regressions than single-agent therapy, while maintaining tolerability if each component has an adequate therapeutic index.

Preclinical studies with PRMT5 inhibitors combined with mutant-selective RAS inhibitors showed greater growth suppression, impaired cell division, tumor regression, and delayed tumor outgrowth compared with either agent alone.
Tango has presented preclinical work supporting the combination of vopimetostat with zoldonrasib (RVMD), showing more durable tumor regression, as well as with the EGFRi osimertinib (Tagrisso).

RAS serves as a central node in the RAS/RAF/MAPK pathway, which holds a key role in regulating cell behavior by relaying extracellular signals to the nucleus to control cell growth, proliferation, and differentiation. Dysregulation of the pathway through gain-of-function mutations in the cascade is a frequent driver of cancer formation.

The RAS family of proteins, including KRAS, NRAS and HRAS, are small GTPases that function as switches, alternating between GDP-bound (OFF) and GTP-bound (ON) states. Activation can be triggered by various stimuli. In the normal state, it is recruited to the plasma membrane following stimulation by growth factors, which leads GEF to exchange GDP for GTP turning the switch ON. In the ON state, RAS interacts with a diverse set of effectors, including the RAF proteins and PI3K, both of which are central regulators of cell functions including growth, metabolism, motility, and proliferation

title_content.content: Why is the dara with Daraxonrasib better than Zoldonrasib

paragraph_content.content: One question that came up from the data was about the worse performance for the zoldonrasib combo, considering it has generally shown similar efficacy in the G12D population as a monotherapy. While daraxonrasib inhibits mutant RAS in many subtypes as well as the WT protein, zoldonrasib only targets the G12D allele (which was a prerequisite to enter the trial). The goal of the combo is to target two separate pathways that cancer cells depend on. Zoldonrasib has very little activity against WT RAS and preclinical data supports the idea that targeting the mutant allele can lead to compensatory upregulation of WT or other mutant forms of RAS. This could potentially explain the higher efficacy seen with dara in the combo. Another explanation by management was that the ECOG status for the G12D cohort was worse than that for the dara population (see table above).

paragraph_content.content: Preclinical work by Tango showed that to achieve maximum monotherapy efficacy could require exposure levels so high they could also inhibit WT PRMT5 limiting the therapeutic window. As glioblastoma (GBM) is one of the cancer types with high MTAP deletion prevalence, it made sense to develop a drug with adequate brain exposure. To achieve proper brain penetration, the ratio of unbound brain-to-plasma
(\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{p,uu}})

is a key parameter to predict the levels of peripheral exposure needed to achieve target brain exposures and would ideally be close to 1 to not affect the therapeutic window. For TNG908 this ratio was predicted to be 0.9 but the 15x selectivity vs WT was assumed to not be high enough and so it wouldn't be possible to achieve adequate CNS concentrations. Based on this, Tango discontinued the TNG908 trial in November 2024.
Tango aimed to generate a molecule that can achieve brain exposure higher than the MTAP-deleted
but lower than the WT
in the periphery to reduce on-target PRMT5 tox in non-tumor cells.

The preclinical data described below show that TNG456 has high potential to be brain penetrant in humans based on preclinical in vitro and in vivo data. Based on this, in May 2025, Tango started enrolling patients in the Ph 1/2 clinical trial for TNG456 as a monotherapy. The trial is currently in the dose escalation phase and assuming favorable monotherapy data, a combination with abemaciclib (Eli Lilly's CDK4/6i aka Verzenio) will be initiated. An update has been guided to 2H26.
Glioblastoma, considered the most aggressive primary brain tumor in adults, has an incidence of
\sim 12\mathrm{K}
cases a year (3.2/100K) in the US or
of all primary brain and CNS tumors and

of malignant brain tumors. The WHO classifies GBM as IDH WT Grade 4 astrocytoma. GBM originates from glial cells and is characterized by high genomic instability leading to a highly heterogeneous presentation. Prognosis remains poor with an OS of 14-16 months following SoC and a 5 year survival rate of

Current SoC for GBM involves surgical resection followed by radiotherapy and chemotherapy with temozolomide (TMZ), an oral alkylating agent. Complete surgical removal is difficult due to tumor infiltration and anatomical proximity to important brain regions. TMZ efficacy is limited by tumor resistance and systemic tox including myelosuppression.

While we could not find any large databases describing MTAP deletion prevalence in GBM, in one study, a sample of 423 cases showed 45.6% had MTAP deletion, while in another there were 33.5% MTAP deletion samples out of 167 GBMs.

In addition to Tango, preclinical work with navlimetostat (previously MRTX-1719) showed strong anti-tumor activity in MTAP-deleted glioma cells. This proved more difficult in vivo as the presence of non-malignant, MTAP-WT cells in the tumor microenvironment can metabolize extracellular MTA, reducing its local concentration and reducing the inhibition it applies to PRMT5.

In a recent Journal of Medicinal Chemistry paper from May 2026 (link), Tango describes the development of TNG456. TNG456 showed no off-target activity against a panel of 40 methyltransferases other than PRMT5 and no other potential off-target binding against 78 known off-target assays. In cell viability assays with cell pairs that were either MTAP WT or MTAP-deleted, TNG456 showed an average of 55x selectivity for the MTAP-deleted cells.

paragraph_content.content: Overall, these assays support TNG456 monotherapy activity in MTAP-deleted tumors. As discussed earlier, since MTAP deletion is usually accompanied by CDKN2A deletion, these cancers may have increased CDK4/6 activity. The CDKN2A locus on chromosome 9p21 encodes two tumor suppressors, p16INK4a and p14ARF. Normally, p16INK4a sequesters CDK4 and CDK6, keeping pRb in an active, hypophosphorylated state. In the absence of p16INK4a, CDK4 and CDK6 bind to cyclin D and phosphorylate Rb which then releases E2F promoting the G1-to-S phase transition of the cell cycle.

This means that cells with the 9p21 deletion exhibit both MTAP deletion, rendering them sensitive to PRMT5 inhibition, and have a reliance on CDK4/6 making them sensitive to its inhibition. There are multiple approved CDK4/6 inhibitors, including palbociclib, ribociclib and abemaciclib. Since these are two discrete susceptibility pathways, similar to RAS, it makes sense that targeting both would be synergistic.

paragraph_content.content: Based on this, Tango tested TNG456 in combination with abemaciclib, a brain-penetrant CDK4/6i, to see if it enhances anti-tumor activity. In the MTAP-deleted AM38 GBM CDX model, neither TNG456 or abemaciclib induced tumor regression, but the combo showed anti-tumor activity. Similarly, in a GBM PDX model, there was strong synergistic activity where the clinically relevant 90mpk BID TNG456 with a lower sub-therapeutic dose of abemaciclib led to a complete response. This was not repeated when using a sub-therapeutic dose of TNG456 with a clinical dose of abemaciclib. Importantly, abemaciclib is a CYP3A4 substrate, while TNG456 was found not to be, lowering the DDI risk.

paragraph_content.content: Tango Therapeutics (Overweight; Price Target: $46.00)

We have an Overweight rating on TNGX shares. We see TNGX set up well following the strong combinatorial data for its lead PRMT5 inhibitor vopimetostat with RAS inhibitors in 2L+ PDAC which supports its planned Ph 3 clinical trial plans in 1L PDAC. While data is early, the unprecedented efficacy in such a difficult indication supports its penetration into the large portion of PDAC patients with MTAP-deletion. Beyond vopimetostat, Tango's CNS-penetrant PRMT5 inhibitor, TNG456, is currently in Ph 1/2 for the very difficult to treat glioblastoma and provides a meaningful virtual “call option” that we think is not reflected in shares today.

Our Dec 2026 price target of $46 is based on our DCF SOTP calculation. We assume standalone contributions from vopimetostat in 1L PDAC and 2L NSCLC as well as TNG456 contributions in GBM. Our $46 price target consists of $39/share for vopimetostat in 1L PDAC, ~$1/share for vopimetostat in 2L NSCLC, $0.4/share for TNG456 in GBM and the remainder for corporate expenses/pipeline and cash.
